head: 127e782
kind: L8 timing
note: issue #24 decision evidence: NER gate shipped at HEAD (9eda40e); lite first-call 11.7s -> 0.0s; regex locks unaffected (5/9 spans)

head: 70178f2
kind: false-positive rate on known-human ESL student writing, by subgroup
corpus: ELLIPSE train split (Crossley et al. 2023), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 3904 essays >=60 words
note: FIRST RUN of the audit position (docs/strategy-the-audit-position.md). Two findings. (1) untell's OWN lite tier flags 97.4% of known-human ESL student essays at its shipped 0.30 threshold; the documented lite figure was 30% on conversational prose. (2) NO subgroup ratio separated at 95% confidence at any threshold, so this corpus shows a catastrophic overall false-positive rate and NO demonstrated per-group disparity. At 0.30 the detector is saturated and disparity is unmeasurable rather than absent, which is why the sweep exists.

head: c2a4c80
kind: false-positive rate by rated English proficiency, known-human ESL essays
corpus: ELLIPSE train split, 3904 essays >=60 words, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
note: The axis that separates. At threshold 0.50 the lite tier's FPR rises MONOTONICALLY across all six reportable proficiency levels, 33.7% -> 53.1%, worst at the HIGHEST proficiency, 1.57x, Wilson intervals separate. That inverts the literature's perplexity story, in which low-proficiency writers are flagged most: a tells-based detector keys on polish, so the most fluent learners look most machine-like to it. At threshold 0.70 the ordering is NOT monotonic and the worst group flips to the LOWEST proficiency (6.2% vs 1.9%, 3.25x, separated). So which group a detector fails depends on where its threshold is set, and a single-threshold audit would have reported one direction and missed the reversal.

head: c115a26
kind: which half of perplexity_burstiness drives the proficiency disparity
note: Both components fall monotonically with proficiency and they pull OPPOSITE ways. Common-word ratio falling means richer vocabulary, which reads as MORE human and protects stronger writers -- the perplexity account in the literature, behaving as predicted. Burstiness CV falling means more uniform sentence lengths, which reads as MORE machine-like. Burstiness wins: FPR rises with proficiency. So the burstiness term penalises writing maturity. Corrects an earlier claim in the strategy doc that the lite tier was tells-keyed rather than perplexity-keyed; it is perplexity_burstiness and is exactly what it says.

head: 29b76b1
kind: held-out replication of the proficiency false-positive gap
corpus: ELLIPSE train (3904) vs held-out test split (2571), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
note: Banded low (<=2.5) vs high (>=3.5) proficiency at threshold 0.50. Overall FPR was 38.7% on BOTH splits and per-level rates tracked within a point wherever n>300. The gap separates at 95% on both. NOTE what did NOT replicate: strict monotonicity across all six levels, and separation of the top level 4.5 alone (n=55 held-out, ratio 1.42x, intervals overlap). The banded contrast is the claim the data supports; the six-level monotonic version was an artifact of the larger split's sample sizes.

head: 29b76b1
kind: which half of perplexity_burstiness is biased, and in which direction
corpus: ELLIPSE train (n=2519 banded) and held-out (n=1618 banded)
note: THE RESULT. Each component thresholded at its own median so both flag ~half the corpus (equal power). The two halves of ONE detector are biased in OPPOSITE directions against OPPOSITE groups, both separated at 95%, on both splits. Vocabulary penalises LOW-proficiency writers, which is exactly Liang et al.'s perplexity account. Burstiness penalises HIGH-proficiency writers, which the literature has not isolated. They partly cancel in the combined score, so ANY aggregate fairness number for this detector understates both -- and a benchmark that treats the detector as a black box cannot see it. Exposed via `untell-subgroup-audit --ablate`.

head: a63ebb9
kind: do the RAW features carry proficiency, before any detector calibrates them
corpus: ELLIPSE train (low 1056 / high 1463) and held-out (low 673 / high 945)
note: The bias is in the FEATURES, not in untell's calibration. More proficient learners are measurably less bursty (d ~ -0.38, replicated) and use measurably fewer common words (d ~ -0.51, replicated). So any detector treating LOW sentence-length variance as machine-like inherits a penalty on writing maturity, and any detector treating predictable vocabulary as machine-like inherits the opposite penalty -- regardless of implementation. SCOPE: burstiness is the feature GPTZero popularised and still explains publicly, but GPTZero itself migrated to a deep-learning architecture in autumn 2023, so this is NOT a claim about current GPTZero. It applies to detectors that still use the heuristic, which includes untell's own lite tier and much of the open-source tier.

head: ed68ef3
kind: independent-corpus replication: FPR by subgroup on ASAP 2.0
corpus: ASAP 2.0 train split (Crossley et al.), 17,307 source-based essays, CC BY 4.0. Independent of ELLIPSE in task type, sampling and population; carries ell_status, which ELLIPSE cannot because every ELLIPSE writer is a learner.
note: ALL FOUR axes separate at 95%. The ell_status result INVERTS the dominant account: non-ELL writers are flagged MORE than English language learners (32.2% vs 26.7%), on an independent 17,307-essay corpus, where Liang et al. found commercial detectors flagging non-native TOEFL essays at 61%. Consistent with the ELLIPSE proficiency finding and with the burstiness mechanism: more fluent, more evenly-structured prose reads as machine-like to a burstiness-weighted detector. Three of four axes point the same way -- the more advantaged or more fluent writer is flagged more (non-ELL > ELL, not-disadvantaged > disadvantaged, higher proficiency > lower). Disability is the exception and points the other way. SCOPE: this is a burstiness-heavy heuristic detector, NOT a commercial neural one, so it does not contradict Liang et al. about the tools they tested -- it shows this CLASS of detector carries the opposite bias. Two tool defects were found and fixed producing this: 'NA' was being treated as a subgroup (4,019 rows, made the 'best' arm, 2.01x phantom ratio), and a --csv label filter silently dropped ell_status and rendered an empty axis.

head: 2cbe9bc
kind: is the burstiness disparity an artifact of one formula
corpus: ELLIPSE train (proficiency bands) and ASAP 2.0 train (ELL bands)
note: FOUR OF FIVE dispersion measures agree, on BOTH corpora and in the same direction: the more fluent group (higher proficiency in ELLIPSE, non-ELL in ASAP) writes sentences of LESS variable length. CV, raw standard deviation and median absolute deviation all say so directly; normalised entropy says it with the opposite sign because entropy over length proportions is MAXIMISED by uniformity. Only range/mean fails (d +0.059 and -0.108), and it is a max-minus-min statistic dominated by a single outlier sentence. So the disparity is a property of the WRITING, not of untell's CV formula, and any burstiness signal built on a standard dispersion measure inherits it. Effect sizes are smaller on ASAP (0.12-0.31) than ELLIPSE (0.47-0.65), matching the smaller measured disparity there (1.21x vs 1.33x). METHOD NOTE: this run EXCLUDES essays with fewer than 2 sentences, where dispersion is undefined; the shipped detector returns 0.0 for them. That is why ELLIPSE CV reads 0.5309 here against 0.5214 in ellipse-raw-signal-effect-sizes, which included the degenerate cases.

head: 45a3df8
kind: a THIRD signal family: real n-gram perplexity, not the stoplist proxy
model: interpolated bigram/unigram LM (lambda=0.7, add-1 unigram backoff) trained on NLTK Brown + Reuters via raw.githubusercontent: 2,001,501 tokens, 56,424 types, 675,817 bigrams. Independent of both essay corpora. Pure stdlib, no HuggingFace.
note: THE RESULT THAT REVISES THE EARLIER STORY. Real perplexity points the SAME way as burstiness and the OPPOSITE way to untell's common-word-ratio proxy. More fluent writers (high proficiency, non-ELL) produce more PREDICTABLE English, so a genuine LM assigns them LOWER perplexity, which is the 'more machine-like' end. So across three signal families: common-word-ratio penalises LOW proficiency (the Liang-shaped direction), while burstiness AND true perplexity both penalise the MORE FLUENT writer. Two of three point at the more fluent writer. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS REPO: untell's lite 'perplexity' channel is a 120-word stoplist ratio, and on this population it is ANTI-CORRELATED with actual perplexity. It is not a valid stand-in for the thing it is named after, and the earlier decomposition note that read it as 'the perplexity account behaving as predicted' was reading the proxy, not perplexity. LIMITATION, and it is a real one: the LM is 1961 Brown American English plus Reuters newswire, a domain mismatch with school essays. Non-native writing being less predictable to THAT model is partly expected. A modern in-domain LM could differ, and testing one needs weights this environment's egress policy blocks.

head: 8fa7279
kind: THE OPEN QUESTION, ANSWERED: does a real transformer show the same correlation
model: GPT-2 124M, gpt2-lm-head-10.onnx (664,871,060 bytes) from the onnx/models LFS store via media.githubusercontent.com; BPE from OpenAI's published encoder.json + vocab.bpe on GitHub; onnxruntime 1.29.0 from pypi. NO HuggingFace anywhere in the path.
note: ANSWERS the question left open all session. A real 124M-parameter transformer shows the SAME correlation as the bigram LM, and shows it MORE STRONGLY: d -0.671 vs -0.491 on ASAP, and -1.320 vs -0.320 on ELLIPSE, the last of which is a very large effect. Native and more proficient writers produce text a real language model finds MORE predictable, i.e. lower perplexity, i.e. the machine-like end. So the direction is not an artifact of a weak n-gram model over 1961 newswire -- scaling the language model AMPLIFIES it. Any perplexity-based detector, which is most neural detectors, should be expected to flag the more fluent writer more on this population until measured otherwise. HOW IT WAS OBTAINED, because I twice reported it as blocked: huggingface.co and four mirrors are egress-blocked, but the ONNX model zoo keeps GPT-2 in GitHub LFS, and LFS objects for public repos are served by media.githubusercontent.com, which is reachable. The earlier 403 was a github.com URL hitting this session's repo scoping, not an egress denial -- I read one error as the other and stopped. LIMITS: n=250 per group (sampled, seed 0), 384-token cap per essay, GPT-2 small rather than a detector. This is a perplexity SIGNAL, not a detector verdict.

head: fa50650
kind: THIRD corpus, new axis (first language), and a DIRECTION REVERSAL
corpus: PELIC (Pittsburgh English Language Institute Corpus), 17,144 texts >=60 words of 46,204 total. ADULT university ESL, 20+ first languages, classroom tasks. Fetched from GitHub LFS. Different age band, different task and different L1 mix from ELLIPSE and ASAP.
note: NEW AXIS: first language changes the false-positive rate. Arabic 40.9% (n=5818) vs Turkish 29.7% (n=536), 1.38x, separated -- both well sampled. The 2.27x German-vs-Hebrew extreme rests on n=52 and n=61 and should not be the quoted figure. DIRECTION REVERSAL, and it must not be smoothed over: PELIC's proficiency effect runs the OPPOSITE way to ELLIPSE's. Here FPR falls monotonically as level rises (52.9% at level 2 to 36.5% at level 5, 1.45x, separated); in ELLIPSE it ROSE with proficiency (33.2% -> 44.2%). So the direction of the proficiency disparity is NOT a property of the detector alone -- it depends on the population and the task. ELLIPSE is US school students writing full independent essays; PELIC is adult university ESL classroom writing. This strengthens rather than weakens the case for the instrument: you cannot predict who a detector fails from a published result, even a result about the same detector and the same kind of subgroup. It has to be measured on the population that will actually be judged. Gender does not separate here either, consistent with ELLIPSE and ASAP. CAVEAT: PELIC's median text is 23 words, so the >=60-word filter keeps 37% and may select for longer, more elaborated answers.

head: d78b9ba
kind: THE LARGEST DISPARITY FOUND, and it is not demographic
note: At one threshold, published professional prose scores 1.4-3.8% while student writing scores 31.6-39.1% -- roughly a TENFOLD gap, an order of magnitude larger than any subgroup disparity measured in this whole body of work (which topped out at 2.27x, and 1.55x among well-sampled groups). The practical reading: a detector validated on 'human writing' -- which in practice usually means published, edited, professional text -- will look excellent and then fail catastrophically on students, who are the population it is actually deployed against. This is a plausible mechanism for vendors reporting sub-1% false-positive rates that nobody can reproduce in a classroom. CONFOUNDS, and they are substantial: Brown/Gutenberg/Reuters are professionally edited and copyedited, drawn from different genres and registers, and chunked into 350-word slices of longer works, whereas the student corpora are first-draft responses to assigned prompts. Genre, editing and task all differ alongside 'professional vs student', so this is not a clean single-variable contrast. Reuters n=26 has a very wide interval and should not be quoted alone. What the comparison does establish is that the population a detector is validated on can differ from its deployment population by an order of magnitude in false-positive rate.

head: ff4fd20
kind: does the professional-vs-student gap hold at the SHIPPED threshold
note: Yes, and it is starker at the shipped 0.30 threshold than at 0.50. Published prose 25.0% (Brown) and 47.2% (Gutenberg) against 97.4% for student ESL essays. At 0.70 professional prose is at 0.0% while students are still at 3.2%. The gap is present at every operating point tested, so it is not an artifact of threshold choice. Gutenberg scoring worse than Brown at 0.30 is worth noting rather than explaining away: 19th-century literary prose is a genre of its own and the ordering among professional corpora is not stable, only their distance from student writing is.

head: 317dbce
kind: does genre explain the professional-vs-student gap? No -- it widens it
method: Brown genre codes, chunked to ~400 words to match the median student essay (ELLIPSE 402, ASAP 345). cb = press EDITORIAL, argumentative prose, the genre match for student argumentative essays. cg = essays/belles-lettres. ca = press reportage, a narrative control that should NOT match.
note: The genre confound flagged in published-vs-student-fpr does NOT account for the gap. With genre AND length matched -- professional argumentative prose against student argumentative essays, both ~400 words -- the gap at threshold 0.50 is 0.6% vs 38.7%, a 64x ratio, WIDER than the ungenre-matched comparison. Brown editorial is the LOWEST-scoring professional category of the three, so matching the genre made the professionals look better, not worse. REMAINING CONFOUND, which cannot be removed with these corpora: professional published prose is copyedited and these are finished published pieces, where student essays are first drafts. Separating 'professional' from 'edited' needs unpublished professional drafts.

head: 317dbce
kind: what threshold would make the lite tier safe on student writing
note: Turns the defect report into a decision. untell ships 0.30, which yields a 97.4% false-positive rate on ELLIPSE. Holding student FPR to 1% needs 0.775; to 5%, 0.671; to 10%, 0.625. Empirical quantiles of the shipped lite scorer over 3,904 known-human ESL essays. NOT a recommendation to change the default: raising the threshold trades false positives for false negatives and the loop's whole behaviour is calibrated around 0.30. It is the number the maintainer needs in order to choose.

head: a0ea03d
kind: rules out EDITING as the explanation for the professional-vs-student gap
note: Editing was the last confound I said could not be removed without unpublished professional drafts. NLTK ships unedited adult writing -- forum posts, wine reviews, product reviews -- and it scores like professionals, not like students. Firefox forum posts are 2.5% at threshold 0.30 where EDITED Brown editorial is 42.6% and student essays are 97.4%. So unedited-ness is not the driver; if anything the unedited informal writing scores BEST. The ordering at 0.30 is monotonic in something else entirely: informal adult writing (0.0-2.5%) < product reviews (26.2%) < formal published essays (42.6-54.9%) < student essays (97.4%). That is a gradient in ESSAY REGISTER -- formality and structural uniformity -- and it is exactly what the burstiness mechanism predicts, since informal writing has wildly varied sentence lengths and a formal assigned essay is the most uniform text a person produces. So the sharpest statement of the finding is not 'professionals vs students'. It is that this detector penalises the ESSAY FORM, and the essay is precisely the artifact students are required to produce and be judged on. LIMITS: n=64-80 per unedited population, so the intervals are wide; these are informal registers, so register and population still covary in the opposite direction from before.

head: ab2586b
kind: per-population false-positive rate on Liang et al. 2023, the field's canonical bias corpus
note: Liang's ordering reproduces against untell's own lite tier: non-native TOEFL writers worst served at 96.7%, US college admission essays best at 58.6%, 1.65x with separated intervals. Added after reading satyamshivam13/AI_Text_Detector, which had been running this measurement since July 2026 while this repository's strategy doc claimed no such tool existed. Every essay is human-authored, so every flag is an error -- except toefl_gpt4_polished, which is human-authored and machine-EDITED and is labelled so it can be held out. Command: untell-subgroup-audit --corpus liang --tier lite --n 0

head: ab2586b
kind: PAIRED within-writer contrast: the same 91 essays, unedited vs GPT-4 polished
note: The first properly paired contrast in this project: same 91 writers, same prompts, only the editing differs. Unedited 96.7%, GPT-4 polished 78.0%, intervals do not overlap (0.9075 > 0.8530). Passing a non-native writer's essay through GPT-4 makes untell's detector LESS likely to call it AI. Result 14 gives the mechanism: polishing moves the essays DOWN the vocabulary channel (100.0% -> 24.2%) and UP the burstiness channel (46.2% -> 74.7%), and the vocabulary effect dominates.

head: ab2586b
kind: the aggregate error rate falls monotonically with the threshold and the disparity does not
note: Overall FPR 79.2% -> 25.6% -> 2.3% while the worst-vs-best population gap goes 1.65x -> 6.93x. At 0.50 the TOEFL non-native essays are flagged 49.5% (39.4-59.5) against 7.1% (3.1-15.7) for college admission essays. Moving 0.30 to 0.50 looks like an unambiguous improvement on the aggregate; the errors that survive are concentrated on the population already worst served. 0.80 and above are SATURATED -- the detector has stopped flagging enough of anything for a difference to be measurable, which is not the same as fair.

head: ab2586b
kind: the two halves of perplexity_burstiness rank the populations in nearly opposite orders
note: Each channel thresholded at its OWN median, so both flag about half the corpus and neither looks fairer merely by having less room to differ. vocabulary spans 144.93x and burstiness 5.9x, both separated at 95%, and each channel's worst-served population is near the other's best. The channel this package calls 'perplexity' is the fraction of tokens from a 120-word stoplist; it flags EVERY non-native TOEFL essay and 0.7% of Stanford CS224N essays. Command: untell-subgroup-audit --corpus liang --tier lite --n 0 --ablate --band-axis population

head: 22e7fc1
kind: BOTH error rates on real paired human/machine text; withdraws Result 11's threshold recommendation

rows.note: Result 11's recommendation; misses ALL 176 GPT-3 essays

note: 215 human and 176 GPT-3 essays from Liang's own Data_and_Results/GPT_Data, domain-matched to the human ones (CS224N 145v145, college admission 70v31). This document said for weeks that equalised odds was blocked for want of a paired corpus because RAID/MAGE/HC3 are HuggingFace-hosted; the machine half was one directory across from the human half already being loaded. Result 11 recommended 0.775 for a 1% false-positive rate on ELLIPSE. Measured against machine text it catches NOTHING -- the highest score anything in this corpus receives is 0.7655, so the threshold sits above the scorer's entire range. Its 0% FPR is not safety, it is an off switch. With one error rate, 'safe' and 'inert' are the same number. Command: untell-subgroup-audit --corpus liang-paired --n 0 --odds --threshold 0.775

head: 22e7fc1
kind: what the lite tier is actually worth: discrimination is real, calibration is not
note: AUROC 0.8012 against a 0.5 coin flip, so the ranking carries real signal and the problem is calibration rather than discrimination: both classes compress into roughly 0.15-0.65 and overlap heavily, so no threshold separates them and the best achievable total error is 51.5% at 0.43. On this evidence the lite tier is a usable RANKING signal and is not usable as an accusation instrument at any threshold -- which is the answer to 'what should the threshold be', rather than a number to move it to.

head: 22e7fc1
kind: false-positive parity looked acceptable while the false-negative gap was 4.1x and separated
note: The failure equalised_odds was built to catch, observed on real data instead of in a fixture. An FPR-only audit at this operating point reports 1.93x that does not reach significance and concludes there is no demonstrated disparity, while the detector is missing two thirds of the machine-written CS224N essays against one sixth of the college essays. LIMIT: TOEFL has no machine counterpart upstream, so the population this work is most concerned with is exactly the one whose false-negative rate cannot be measured.

head: 67fb4f3
kind: the cheapest possible evasion -- one instruction added to the prompt -- multiplies the miss rate
note: Liang generated each machine arm twice: GPT-3 on the prompt, and GPT-3 on the prompt asked to write in a way that does not look machine-generated. Same model, same prompts, same 176 essays, human arm unchanged so FPR is identical and only the miss rate moves. Both gaps separate at 95%. At the SHIPPED 0.30 the detector flags 68.4% of real students while missing one in ten machine essays that were merely asked to be discreet; at the best-total-error 0.43 it misses half. The attack is one sentence in a prompt -- no tool, no budget, no skill. ROADMAP treats raw evasion strength as unwinnable and that stands, but the reason is stronger than 'the state of the art is ahead': the BASELINE attack already works.

head: 6bd4ff4
kind: Result 12 does not generalise: on a second population LLM editing RAISES the flag rate
note: Result 12 concluded from TOEFL that a language model editing an essay makes it look like a more fluent human. On HewlettStudentEssay_GPTsimplify_88 the effect REVERSES: 88.6% -> 94.3%, d=+0.646. The general claim is withdrawn. The mechanism survives and is not the obvious one -- both treatments move BOTH channels the same way (common-word ratio down, burstiness down), and since higher common-ratio reads machine-like while lower burstiness reads machine-like, the two pull against each other in both cases. The net direction is decided by which movement is larger: TOEFL vocab -0.120 vs burst -0.075 so the score falls; 8th grade vocab -0.086 vs burst -0.188 so it rises. Result 14's opposed channels predict the reversal rather than merely describing a ranking.

head: d5df75d
kind: RETRACTED headline: crossing loses its verdict once the worst-vs-best pick is corrected for the cells it was chosen from
note: 17,307 ASAP essays at 0.50. Originally reported as 2.14x separated, concluding 'cross the axes, single-axis reporting understates'. WITHDRAWN. `separated` compared two groups the data selected, against a plain 95% interval; with 10 reportable cells that pick comes from 45 pairs. Bonferroni (z=3.28) retracts the crossed axis AND race_ethnicity alone at six levels. Only the two-level ell_status axis survives, at 1.21x. The corrected lesson is the opposite: crossing buys resolution and pays for it in power, because the correction scales with cells. Cross axes with FEW levels -- Result 20's 2x2 survives at z=2.64 where this 6x2 does not at z=3.28.

head: 6fc273b
kind: the axis untell held data for and never measured; disability cancels the ELL effect
note: The literature names neurodivergent students as disproportionately flagged. ASAP labels 1,921 essays as identified with a disability and this instrument had never looked -- the axis was not in DEFAULT_AXES, which carries ELLIPSE's column names. It is the FIRST axis in the document where the direction matches the field's expectation; every other one reverses it. The crossed row is the finding: this detector treats ELL status as protective (26.7% vs 32.2%, Result 19) and that protection is absent for students with disabilities -- not-identified ELL 26.0%, identified ELL 36.9%. Neither single axis shows it. Defaults now follow the corpus, because a heading a caller never thinks to request is a group nobody measures. SURVIVES the selection correction on every row -- not because the effect is larger but because the cross is 2x2: four cells, six pairs, z=2.64.

head: af49462
kind: every multi-group claim in the document, re-derived after correcting the separation test

rows.axis: pelic L1 Arabic vs Turkish (hand-picked, z=3.65)
pelic L1 tool worst-vs-best German vs Hebrew

note: `separated` compared the extremes of a set the data chose against a plain 95% interval. Bonferroni over the k(k-1)/2 pairs such a pick could land on: z=1.96 at k=2, 2.94 at 6, 3.41 at 13, 3.65 at 20. Four retractions, all from this session or earlier, none touching a result with a mechanism attached; everything mechanistic survives, including Result 14 clearing a 45-pair correction on a 144.93x spread -- the evidence the test is not merely conservative. PELIC is the notable one: the document had already declined the tool's own 2.27x headline because it rested on n=52 and n=61, and quoted the well-sampled Arabic-vs-Turkish pair instead. The correction retracts the headline and keeps the hand-picked pair at z=3.65. Editorial caution and the statistics agreed independently.

head: 7377c1c
kind: 46 real detectors' own published calibration says one threshold cannot hold a uniform FPR
note: RAID's leaderboard requires every submission to publish, per text domain, the threshold at which its FPR on human text is 5% -- raid/evaluate.py find_threshold fits it separately on each domain's human unattacked texts. A domain-stable detector would report eight near-identical numbers. Median span is 0.610 of the 0-1 range. These tools ship ONE threshold, so a single deployed threshold cannot hold a uniform false-positive rate. Binoculars at 0.030 is the counterexample that makes the other 45 credible. Domain ordering is consistent across detectors (recipes most permissive, books/reviews strictest), so it is a property of the text. Evidence extracted to .claude/probes/raid-per-domain-thresholds.json; the RAID dataset itself is at raid-bench.xyz, which this environment's egress policy denies.

head: 7377c1c
kind: the missing half: FNR on current-model text, against FPR on human students, same prompts
note: The documents said the missing half was DATA not capability: no paired human/machine corpus. Twelve essays were generated on ASAP's own seven assignment prompts at matched length, plainly and with no attempt to evade, and scored against 600 human ASAP essays. No operating point works: at the shipped 0.30 the detector catches all machine text and flags 90.7% of human students; at 0.775 it spares 99.5% of humans and misses 100% of machine text. The machine median (0.374) sits BELOW the human median (0.450) -- this detector scores current-model essays as more human than real student essays. n=12 is small and the generator is a single current model, so this is a demonstration on one detector and one generator, not a general rate.

head: 976529d
kind: attack effectiveness and generator detectability across 46 real detectors

rows.note: BIMODAL -- the mean is the wrong statistic
most domain-STABLE detector in Result 21; robustness does not transfer
every base->chat pair rises: mistral .836->.936, mpt .833->.900, cohere .804->.875. Instruction tuning makes text MORE detectable.

note: RAID submissions publish accuracy at a fixed 5% FPR for every domain x generator x attack combination, 10,749 rows per detector. Homoglyph substitution is the most effective attack by mean, but the mean hides a bimodal shape: median per-detector loss is 0.7% while 14 of 43 lose over 20 points and two fall below 5%. Unicode normalisation before tokenisation defeats it and a third of the field has not done it. This corrects the census's treatment of unicode-trickery as a marginal category. Separately, instruction tuning makes text more detectable in every base/chat pair, and GPT-4 is caught more easily than base Cohere -- the strongest model is not the hardest to catch.

head: 0aa7adf
kind: the leaderboard's remaining axes, and the calibration assumption behind every number on it

rows.note: NEGATIVE result: AUROC does not flatter here
every leaderboard figure assumes per-domain threshold fitting

note: Sampling and repetition penalty both cost 4-7 points of detectability, same direction as the generator finding: more predictable text is more detectable. AUROC does NOT overstate operating-point accuracy on this benchmark, which is a common critique that happens not to apply -- worth recording because it costs nothing. The reframing: RAID's evaluator defaults to per_domain_tuning=True, so a median detector's 97.2% accuracy at 5% FPR was earned with a threshold fitted separately per domain. No deployed detector swaps thresholds by document type, and Result 21 measures those thresholds spanning a median 0.610 of the range. The published numbers are an upper bound under conditions users do not have. This does NOT quantify the shortfall -- that needs score distributions the leaderboard does not publish.

head: 1b6f77a
kind: WRONG -- abstentions counted as false negatives; see the corrected recipe

rows.note: flagged 0 of 246 humans and missed 249 of 250 machine texts: INERT, not fair

rows.caveat: the FPR column on this axis is confounded: each M4 file pairs one generator with one domain, so BLOOMZ and davinci both show arxiv's 61.6%. Only FNR is about generators.

note: WITHDRAWN. This run read score_text's `max` without checking `scored`, so the 236-of-240 Urdu rows the detector correctly REFUSED to score were counted as machine text it had missed. M4 ships a paired corpus in its GitHub repo -- prompt, human answer, machine answer per record -- which docs/detector-fairness-measured.md listed as something it did not have. Overall the lite tier misses 40.7% of machine text while flagging 25.8% of humans. The headline is the language axis and it is not a fairness finding: on Urdu the detector flags nothing and misses everything, because its first channel is the fraction of tokens from a 120-WORD ENGLISH STOPLIST and non-English text contains almost none. It returns a low score rather than abstaining, so a user reads 'this is human' where the truth is 'this instrument produced no evidence'. A false clear with no warning is worse than a false positive because nothing in the output invites doubt. Command: python -m eval.subgroup_audit with load_m4; see .claude/probes for the run script.

kind: the audit's missing half, on a real paired corpus, with abstentions counted separately

rows.caveat: FPR on this axis is confounded with domain; only FNR is about generators

note: Corrects m4-equalised-odds, which counted abstentions as misses. The finding is the opposite of the withdrawn one: the detector's refusal is SCRIPT-gated, not language-gated. Its word regex is [A-Za-z']+, so Arabic script yields no tokens and it opts out on 99.8% of Urdu, marks the result scored:False and warns -- the safety behaviour works. German and Indonesian tokenise fine, so it scores them with full confidence and misses 82.8% and 74.8% of the machine text against 21.4% for English. The guard fires where the text is OBVIOUSLY foreign and stays silent where it is not; Latin-script non-English is the dangerous case because nothing in the output distinguishes a confident German verdict from a confident English one.
